hypotheses.title: Anyone can call nukeFromOrbit to force-block a sanctioned account
hypotheses.description: `nukeFromOrbit(address)` has no access modifier — it is callable by any external actor. It only checks `_isSanctioned(accountAddress)` (a public Chainalysis query) and then calls `_blockAccount`, which queues the victim's full balance for withdrawal and moves it to escrow. The function is intended to be a permissionless keeper action, but the effect is that any caller can force a sanctioned lender's funds into a withdrawal batch at an arbitrary time, changing their interest accrual and locking them out of normal withdrawal flow.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a lender address that is flagged on Chainalysis (or the borrower's sentinel reports sanctioned). 2. Attacker calls `nukeFromOrbit(victim)` directly. 3. `_blockAccount` queues the victim's entire scaled balance into the current pending withdrawal batch, burning their market tokens and moving the normalized amount to escrow. 4. Victim's funds are now frozen in escrow until sanctions are lifted, and the victim loses any interest that would have accrued had the balance remained.
hypotheses.impact: Forced liquidation of a sanctioned lender's position at an attacker-chosen time; loss of accrued interest and loss of control over withdrawal timing. Funds are not stolen but are frozen in escrow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `nukeFromOrbit` to the borrower (or a trusted keeper role), or at minimum require that the account is sanctioned and that the caller has a legitimate interest (e.g., borrower).

hypotheses.title: Missing minimum-out / slippage on deposit and withdrawal amounts
hypotheses.description: `depositUpTo` accepts any `amount` and mints scaled tokens based on the current `scaleFactor`, but there is no `minSharesOut` parameter. A lender calling `depositUpTo` in a block where interest has accrued (or where a pending withdrawal batch is being processed) can receive fewer market tokens than expected, and `deposit` only checks `amount == actualAmount` (which is about max supply, not share price). Similarly `queueWithdrawal`/`queueFullWithdrawal` accept a `normalizedAmount` but do not enforce a minimum payout, so a lender can be forced to accept a worse exchange rate than intended.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a victim's pending `depositUpTo`/`queueWithdrawal` transaction in the mempool. 2) Attacker front-runs by calling `updateState()` (or any state-mutating function) to accrue interest and/or process an expired withdrawal batch, changing `scaleFactor` and `normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals`. 3) Victim's transaction executes at the new, worse rate with no revert because no min-out parameter exists.
hypotheses.impact: Lenders receive fewer market tokens or fewer underlying assets than intended; value is effectively transferred to the borrower/other lenders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add explicit `minSharesOut` / `minAmountOut` parameters to deposit and withdrawal entry points and revert if the computed amount is below the minimum.

hypotheses.title: Griefing executeWithdrawal via queued dust from sanctioned account
hypotheses.description: executeWithdrawals() loops over a caller-supplied array of accounts and expiries calling _executeWithdrawal for each, and _executeWithdrawal reverts with NullWithdrawalAmount if the computed normalizedAmountWithdrawn is zero. Any single pair with zero owed amount reverts the entire batch call, so an array containing a stale or already-withdrawn entry blocks processing for all other entries.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker (or any lender) passes an array mixing valid entries with an already-fully-withdrawn pair; the loop hits the fully-drawn pair, _executeWithdrawal computes zero and reverts NullWithdrawalAmount, so the whole batch call reverts and no entries execute. The attacker can repeat forever, and since this only exists as a convenience batch and single executeWithdrawal still works, this is Medium at most.
hypotheses.impact: Caller-supplied batch execution of withdrawals always fails when any entry has zero amount, forcing per-entry calls; griefers can prevent aggregated withdrawal processing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip entries where normalizedAmountWithdrawn == 0 instead of reverting, or make single-execute the documented path.

hypotheses.title: WildcatSanctionsEscrow.releaseEscrow is permanently frozen for sanctioned account
hypotheses.description: releaseEscrow() requires !IWildcatSanctionsSentinel(sentinel).isSanctioned(borrower, account) before transferring. If the account remains on the Chainalysis list and the borrower (possibly itself sanctioned) can no longer or never calls overrideSanction, the escrow funds are permanently stuck. Because sanctions status is controlled by an external list and can be permanent, escrowed funds cannot be recovered by any untrusted actor except the borrower's override.
hypotheses.attackPath: A sanctioned lender's market balance is nuked into an escrow; if the borrower becomes inactive/sanctioned, or refuses to override, the account cannot call releaseEscrow (blocked by canReleaseEscrow == false) and no third party can recover the funds. The escrow has no other withdrawal path.
hypotheses.impact: Escrowed user funds are permanently frozen with no recovery.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a permissioned recovery path (e.g., arch controller or a time-locked beneficiary) or allow the escrow to be released to the account via a grace mechanism.

hypotheses.title: WildcatMarketBase._getMarketParameters trusts caller() without validation
hypotheses.description: The market constructor calls `_getMarketParameters()` which does a `staticcall` to `caller()` (the factory) with selector `0x04032dbb` (`getMarketParameters`) and copies 0x260 bytes of returndata into memory. It checks `returndatasize() == 0x260` and that the call succeeds, but does not verify that `caller()` is actually the expected factory. Since the market is deployed via `create2` from the factory, `caller()` is the factory during construction. However, the factory's `getMarketParameters()` reads from transient storage `_tmpMarketParameters`, which is set by `_setTmpMarketParameters` before `create2WithStoredInitCode`. If the factory's transient storage is not set (e.g. if a market is deployed via a different path, or if the factory is called in a way that doesn't set transient storage), the market would be constructed with zeroed parameters. More critically, the market constructor does not validate that `parameters.asset`, `parameters.borrower`, etc. are non-zero. A malicious actor who can cause a market to be deployed with zeroed parameters (e.g. by calling `create2WithStoredInitCode` directly on the factory's init code storage, or by manipulating the factory) could create a market with `asset = address(0)`, `borrower = address(0)`, etc. The factory's `_deployMarket` sets transient storage before deployment, but the market constructor's trust in `caller()` is absolute.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker obtains the market init code storage address (public via `marketInitCodeStorage`). 2. Attacker calls `create2` directly with the init code and a salt, bypassing the factory's `_deployMarket`. 3. The market constructor calls `caller()` (the attacker) with `getMarketParameters` selector. 4. The attacker's contract returns 0x260 bytes of crafted data, setting `asset`, `borrower`, `sentinel`, etc. to attacker-controlled values. 5. The market is deployed with attacker-controlled parameters, potentially allowing the attacker to drain funds or manipulate the market.
hypotheses.impact: An attacker can deploy a market with arbitrary parameters by directly calling `create2` with the market init code, bypassing the factory's validation. This could lead to a market with a malicious asset, borrower, or sentinel, enabling theft of funds from users who interact with the fake market.
hypotheses.recommendation: In the market constructor, verify that `msg.sender` is the expected factory (e.g. by checking against a known factory address or by validating the returned parameters against expected values). Alternatively, pass parameters as constructor arguments instead of reading them via `staticcall`.

hypotheses.title: grantRole allows any approved provider to overwrite credentials of accounts from other providers
hypotheses.description: `_grantRole` allows a caller to overwrite an existing credential if `newExpiry > oldExpiry`, even when the caller is a different provider than the one that granted the old credential. This means any approved role provider can "steal" a lender's credential from another provider by granting a longer expiry, and can also revoke it later via `revokeRole` (since `status.lastProvider` is now the attacker). A malicious or compromised provider can thus take over any lender's access status and revoke it at will.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker is an approved role provider (added by borrower). 2. Attacker calls `grantRole(victim, timestamp)` with a timestamp giving a longer expiry than the victim's current credential. 3. `_grantRole` sees `newExpiry > oldExpiry` and overwrites `status.lastProvider` to the attacker. 4. Attacker now calls `revokeRole(victim)` to revoke the victim's access, or uses the takeover to control the victim's status.
hypotheses.impact: A malicious provider can revoke access for any lender whose credential it can outlast, effectively censoring lenders. This is a trust escalation beyond the intended "provider grants its own users" model.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only allow a provider to overwrite a credential if it is the same provider as `status.lastProvider`, or if the previous provider is no longer supported. Remove the `newExpiry > oldExpiry` bypass for different providers.

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer / rebasing asset breaks totalAssets accounting
hypotheses.description: `_depositUpTo` transfers `amount` via `safeTransferFrom` and credits `scaledAmount = scaleAmount(amount)` to the depositor, assuming the market received exactly `amount`. For fee-on-transfer tokens, the market receives less than `amount`, so `totalAssets()` is lower than the sum of normalized balances, causing `liquidityRequired()` to exceed `totalAssets()` and the market to appear delinquent. Similarly, rebasing tokens change `totalAssets()` without updating `scaledTotalSupply`, breaking `borrowableAssets` and `withdrawableProtocolFees`. The factory does not blacklist such assets by default (only owner-curated blacklist).
hypotheses.attackPath: A borrower deploys a market with a fee-on-transfer or rebasing token (not blacklisted). Lenders deposit; the market's `totalAssets` diverges from `scaledTotalSupply * scaleFactor`. A lender can then queue a withdrawal that, when executed, transfers more than the market's real balance allows, or the borrower can borrow more than intended because `borrowableAssets` uses inflated `totalAssets`.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency — last withdrawers cannot be paid; protocol fees over-withdrawn; borrower over-borrows.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure actual received amount (`balanceOf` before/after) in `_depositUpTo` and credit that; document/blacklist rebasing and fee-on-transfer tokens.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy via hooks in _getUpdatedState / view functions
hypotheses.description: The market's view functions (e.g. `totalSupply`, `balanceOf`, `scaledBalanceOf`, `currentState`, `getWithdrawalBatch`) call `_calculateCurrentState()` which reads `totalAssets()` and computes state, while state-changing functions like `_transfer` invoke `hooks.onTransfer` BEFORE updating `_accounts`/`_writeState`. A hook contract (`AccessControlHooks.onTransfer`/`onDeposit`) performs external calls to role providers (e.g. `_tryValidateCredential` → `validateCredential` on an untrusted provider address supplied in calldata via hooksData). During that external call, the attacker's provider contract can re-enter a market view function; because the market state has not yet been written (still pre-transfer), the view returns stale `scaledTotalSupply`/balances that don't reflect the in-flight debit/credit. Any downstream protocol reading those views gets inconsistent values.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a malicious role provider registered by borrower (or uses an existing pull provider that is malicious). Attacker calls `transfer`/`deposit` with crafted `hooksData` containing the malicious provider address and data. The hook calls `validateCredential` on the attacker's provider; the provider re-enters `market.totalSupply()`/`getWithdrawalBatch(...)` or `_calculateCurrentState` while the market is mid-update, capturing stale accounting. Attacker then uses that stale view in a dependent integration (lending/liquidator) to exploit mispriced state.
hypotheses.impact: Downstream integrations that rely on market view functions during a `transfer`/`deposit` get inconsistent `scaledTotalSupply`/balances, enabling mispriced liquidations, under-collateralized borrows, or withdrawal-batch manipulation against those integrations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either apply state writes before invoking hooks, or add a reentrancy guard that also blocks view functions (extend `nonReentrantView` to also be aware of pending state-changing calls), so views during hook execution revert instead of returning stale data.

hypotheses.title: pushProtocolFeeBipsUpdates stops whole batch on a single misbehaving market
hypotheses.description: The loop calls each market with the fee setter and reverts entire transaction if any single market reverts (e.g. market has been closed/removed, or its setProtocolFeeBips has been blocked). Since the factory admin/borrower cannot skip a bad market, one stuck market freezes the fee update for all subsequent markets in the array.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any borrower deploys a market whose setProtocolFeeBips reverts (e.g. market migrated to closed state through normal use, or its per-market setter is paused), then the operator's call to pushProtocolFeeBipsUpdates reverts on that entry, and all later markets never receive fee updates.
hypotheses.impact: Fee policy changes cannot be propagated; fee updates are blocked for many markets indefinitely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip failed markets and continue iteration (emit a per-market failure event), or allow a start index to skip.

hypotheses.title: Role provider credential timestamp is not bound to chain or contract
hypotheses.description: The credential validation path forwards `hooksData` (provider address + opaque bytes) to the role provider's `validateCredential(address,bytes)` and accepts any returned `uint32` timestamp as a valid credential. The hooks contract does not include `address(this)`, `block.chainid`, or the market address in the data passed to the provider, and does not verify that the provider's returned timestamp was actually signed for this specific hooks instance. A provider that signs a credential for one market/hooks instance (or one chain) will have that same signature accepted on any other market using the same hooks instance, because the hooks contract only checks `credentialTimestamp <= block.timestamp` and `provider.calculateExpiry(credentialTimestamp) >= block.timestamp`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid credential signature from an approved role provider for a low-value or test market (or on a testnet fork of the same hooks instance). 2) Attacker replays the same `hooksData` suffix on a different market that uses the same `AccessControlHooks` instance (or on the same market on a forked chain). 3) `_tryValidateCredential` calls the provider, which returns the same timestamp, and the hooks contract accepts it, marking the attacker as a known lender and granting deposit/transfer access.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized lenders gain deposit and transfer access to restricted markets, bypassing KYC/allowlist controls and potentially enabling sanctioned or unvetted parties to enter the market.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `address(this)`, `block.chainid`, and the market address in the data passed to `validateCredential`, and require the provider to sign over those values so credentials cannot be replayed across markets or chains.

hypotheses.title: Temporary reserve ratio can be gamed to avoid reserve requirements
hypotheses.description: The `onSetAnnualInterestAndReserveRatioBips` hook allows the borrower to reduce the annual interest rate, which triggers a temporary increase in the reserve ratio. However, the logic for canceling or expiring the temporary reserve ratio can be gamed. If the borrower reduces the rate, then immediately increases it back to the original (or higher), the temporary reserve ratio is canceled (`canCancel` is true if `annualInterestBips >= tmp.originalAnnualInterestBips`). This means the borrower can repeatedly reduce and restore the rate to avoid the temporary reserve ratio increase, effectively bypassing the intended penalty for reducing the rate. The check `canCancel` only requires the new rate to be >= the original rate, so a borrower can set the rate to the original value and cancel the temporary reserve ratio without waiting for expiry.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Borrower reduces annual interest rate, triggering temporary reserve ratio increase. 2. Borrower immediately calls `setAnnualInterestAndReserveRatioBips` with the original rate. 3. `canCancel` is true, so the temporary reserve ratio is deleted and the original reserve ratio is restored. 4. Borrower has effectively reduced the rate and restored it without any penalty.
hypotheses.impact: Borrower avoids the intended reserve ratio increase, potentially leaving the market undercollateralized during the period of reduced rates.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the temporary reserve ratio to persist for a minimum period, or prevent cancellation until the expiry has passed.

hypotheses.title: WildcatMarketBase._isSanctioned ignores return value of sentinel call
hypotheses.description: `_isSanctioned()` performs a `staticcall` to the sentinel contract and checks `returndatasize() == 0x20` and that the call succeeds. However, it does not verify that the returned value is a valid boolean (0 or 1). If the sentinel returns a non-boolean value (e.g. a large number), `result := mload(0)` would set `result` to a truthy value, potentially blocking or allowing accounts incorrectly. More importantly, the function reverts if the call fails, which means if the sentinel is upgraded or becomes unavailable, all market operations that call `_isSanctioned` (e.g. `_getAccount`, `executeWithdrawal`) would revert, freezing the market. The sentinel is immutable in the market, so it cannot be upgraded, but the sentinel's `isSanctioned` function calls `isFlaggedByChainalysis` which calls the Chainalysis sanctions list — if that external call fails, the sentinel reverts, and the market reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker causes the Chainalysis sanctions list to revert (e.g. by calling a function that consumes all gas, or if the Chainalysis contract is paused/upgraded). 2. All market operations that call `_isSanctioned` (deposit, withdraw, transfer) revert. 3. Users cannot withdraw their funds.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service — users cannot deposit, withdraw, or transfer market tokens if the sentinel or Chainalysis contract reverts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Handle the case where the sentinel call fails gracefully (e.g. treat as not sanctioned) or use a try/catch pattern. Alternatively, cache the sanction status or use a fallback mechanism.

hypotheses.title: executeWithdrawal allows anyone to trigger withdrawal for any account
hypotheses.description: `executeWithdrawal(address accountAddress, uint32 expiry)` is `public` with no caller restriction. Any external actor can execute a pending withdrawal on behalf of any account once the batch has expired. While the funds go to the correct account (or escrow if sanctioned), this lets an attacker force a sanctioned account's withdrawal into escrow, or force a lender to receive funds at a time of the attacker's choosing (e.g., to manipulate their tax/accounting or to grief them by triggering escrow creation).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker waits for a withdrawal batch to expire. 2. Attacker calls `executeWithdrawal(victim, expiry)` for a victim who has not yet withdrawn. 3. If the victim is sanctioned, funds are sent to escrow and the victim is blocked; otherwise the victim receives funds involuntarily. 4. Attacker can repeat for many victims in one tx via `executeWithdrawals`.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: forced escrow creation for sanctioned accounts, forced fund receipt, and potential DoS of a victim's intended withdrawal path (e.g., if they wanted to keep funds in the market).
hypotheses.recommendation: Either restrict `executeWithdrawal` to `msg.sender == accountAddress` (or an approved operator), or explicitly document and accept permissionless execution as intended behavior.

hypotheses.title: Rounding in _applyWithdrawalBatchPayment can leave dust that blocks closeMarket
hypotheses.description: `normalizedAmountPaid` is computed with `mulDiv` (round down) while `scaledAmountBurned` is derived from `scaleAmount(availableLiquidity)` which uses `rayDiv` (round half up). When the batch is fully paid, `scaledAmountBurned == scaledAmountOwed`, but the normalized amount credited to `normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals` may be slightly less than the true normalized value of the burned scaled tokens. The comment acknowledges this is intentional to allow batches to finish, but the residual dust accumulates in `normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals` vs actual assets and can cause `closeMarket`'s `availableLiquidity = currentlyHeld - (normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals + accruedProtocolFees)` to underflow or leave a nonzero `scaledPendingWithdrawals` that reverts `revert_CloseMarketWithUnpaidWithdrawals()`.
hypotheses.attackPath: A lender queues a withdrawal of a tiny amount (e.g., 1 wei) in a batch. Due to rounding, the batch's `normalizedAmountPaid` is 0 while `scaledAmountBurned` is nonzero, or vice versa. Repeated across many small withdrawals, the borrower's `closeMarket()` reverts because `scaledPendingWithdrawals != 0` even though all batches appear paid, or `availableLiquidity` underflows.
hypotheses.impact: Market cannot be closed; borrower's funds locked; lenders' withdrawals may be permanently stuck in a batch that can never fully settle.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure `normalizedAmountPaid` is computed consistently with `scaledAmountBurned` (e.g., use `normalizeAmount` and accept the dust in the batch, or track dust explicitly), and make `closeMarket` tolerant of residual scaled dust.

hypotheses.title: `getAvailableWithdrawalAmount` uses stale batch when expiry equals pending batch
hypotheses.description: The function calls `_calculateCurrentState()` which returns `pendingBatch` only when the batch is expired and processed. If `expiry == pendingBatchExpiry` but the batch is not yet expired (or `pendingBatchExpiry` is 0), the code falls through to `_withdrawalData.batches[expiry]` which is the stored (stale) batch. Because `_calculateCurrentState` only returns a non-zero `pendingBatchExpiry` for expired batches, a caller querying an in-flight batch gets the stored `normalizedAmountPaid` which may be lower than the actual amount that will be paid once the batch is processed, understating the withdrawable amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A lender queues a withdrawal creating a batch. 2) Before expiry, the borrower repays, increasing available liquidity. 3) A third party (or the lender) calls `getAvailableWithdrawalAmount` and receives a value based on the stale stored batch rather than the current state. 4) Any integrator relying on this view (e.g., a lending protocol using it as collateral valuation) misprices the position.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect view-based accounting; integrators may under- or over-value withdrawal positions, leading to bad liquidations or mispriced collateral.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `expiry == state.pendingWithdrawalExpiry` (regardless of expiry status), return the batch computed from `_calculateCurrentState` rather than the stored batch.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy into market from untrusted role provider during deposit hook
hypotheses.description: `_depositUpTo` executes `hooks.onDeposit(...)` (which may call an untrusted role provider's `validateCredential`) BEFORE `asset.safeTransferFrom` and before writing the updated `_accounts[msg.sender]` and `_writeState`. Although `nonReentrant` protects the market's state-changing functions, the hook can invoke a *different* market contract that shares the same borrower/hook configuration or any other contract that reads the market's pre-update state via `_calculateCurrentState`. The check `if (scaledAmount == 0) revert` happens before the hook, but the actual balance/supply mutations happen after the external call, so a malicious provider can observe/modify dependent state mid-deposit.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker crafts `hooksData` pointing to their own provider implementing `validateCredential`, which re-enters an external contract (e.g. a second market or a protocol reading the first market's `balanceOf`) to act on the not-yet-updated balance, then returns a valid timestamp to pass the hook. The deposit then completes normally and the attacker exits with the extracted value.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent market state observable mid-deposit allows dependent protocols/markets to be drained or to misprice deposits, potentially causing loss of funds in integrations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply all state mutations (account balance, scaledTotalSupply, `_writeState`) BEFORE invoking the external `hooks.onDeposit` call, or move hook invocation after `asset.safeTransferFrom` and state writes.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy from executeWithdrawal hook (onExecuteWithdrawal) before state write
hypotheses.description: `_executeWithdrawal` calls `hooks.onExecuteWithdrawal(...)` before decrementing `state.normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals`, updating `status.normalizedAmountWithdrawn`, and before `_writeState`. `AccessControlHooks.onExecuteWithdrawal` is a no-op, but hooks are pluggable — a hooks template with `useOnExecuteWithdrawal` enabled can call arbitrary code. Because `executeWithdrawals` in a single tx processes multiple accounts using a cached `state` and one write at the end, a reentrant call into any market function that reads `_calculateCurrentState` sees the withdrawal not yet subtracted from `normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals`, and the account's `normalizedAmountWithdrawn` still unset, so it appears the withdrawal is still owed.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (as marketplace hooks template with `useOnExecuteWithdrawal`) triggers `executeWithdrawal`, whose hook re-enters `getAvailableWithdrawalAmount` for the same account; this returns the full amount again. The attacker uses the stale view in a dependent protocol to double-count the claim, or triggers `repayAndProcessUnpaidWithdrawalBatches` to reallocate liquidity.
hypotheses.impact: Stale view mid-execution can lead dependent protocols to over-credit the user (double-counted unclaimed withdrawal), causing accounting discrepancies and potential loss of funds in integrations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the status/state writes (decrement `normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals`, set `status.normalizedAmountWithdrawn`, `_writeState`) before invoking `hooks.onExecuteWithdrawal`, or gate view functions with `nonReentrantView` that also reverts while a state-changing call is in flight.

hypotheses.title: repayAndProcessUnpaidWithdrawalBatches can be DoS'd via satSub mismatch
hypotheses.description: In the loop, availableLiquidity = availableLiquidity.satSub(normalizedAmountPaid). If _processUnpaidWithdrawalBatch returns normalizedAmountPaid greater than availableLiquidity (which can happen due to rounding in mulDiv when scaledAvailableLiquidity rounds down but normalizedAmountPaid rounds up relative to it, or because of accumulation across batches), satSub silently returns 0 and the loop exits. More importantly, if the queue-driven amount causes state.normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals to grow beyond totalAssets, subsequent iterations can revert with underflow inside fee/withdrawal math.
hypotheses.attackPath: A griefer queues withdrawals in many small batches and repeatedly forces partial repayment; rounding in _applyWithdrawalBatchPayment (mulDiv down) makes normalizedAmountPaid diverge from consumed liquidity; satSub masks the difference, so availableLiquidity is set to 0 and later batches never get processed through this permissionless path.
hypotheses.impact: Stuck unpaid batches persist despite available liquidity; lenders cannot get their withdrawals processed through the batch function; wrong accounting accumulates.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use checked subtraction and assert normalizedAmountPaid <= availableLiquidity, or clamp inside _processUnpaidWithdrawalBatch.

hypotheses.title: Borrower can permanently block last lender via reserveRatio/debt mismatch + close
hypotheses.description: closeMarket() iterates over all unpaid batches and calls _processUnpaidWithdrawalBatch with the residual availableLiquidity. If any batch cannot be fully paid because available liquidity is consumed by normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals and accruedProtocolFees, the function leaves scaledPendingWithdrawals != 0 and reverts CloseMarketWithUnpaidWithdrawals. However, because the availableLiquidity accounting subtracts only normalizedAmountPaid per batch and never re-checks the total, a griefer/borrower can arrange tiny unclaimed withdrawals such that the loop exhausts liquidity on the first few batches, leaving later ones permanently unpaid, with the borrower calling closeMarket repeatedly and reverting.
hypotheses.attackPath: A borrower queues a full withdrawal of a tiny amount, waits for expiry, executes it so normalizedUnclaimedWithdrawals > 0, then calls closeMarket. The loop processes at most one batch with the shrunk availableLiquidity and reverts on the final check while scaledPendingWithdrawals != 0. Borrower can also hold funds back, and lenders cannot force their batches to be processed through this function.
hypotheses.impact: Market cannot be closed; remaining lenders are stuck; borrower can keep the market in a half-paid state indefinitely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow closeMarket to succeed with unpaid batches, marking them as IOUs, or iterate the queue properly until liquidity or queue is exhausted.

hypotheses.title: Pull provider credential refresh lacks chain/contract binding
hypotheses.description: `_tryGetCredential` calls `IRoleProvider.getCredential(address)` on a pull provider and accepts any returned `uint32` timestamp as a valid credential, provided it is non-zero, not in the future, and not expired. The call does not include `address(this)`, `block.chainid`, or the market address, so a pull provider that returns a credential based on off-chain state (e.g., a signed attestation) will return the same value regardless of which hooks instance or chain is calling. An attacker who is approved on one market can therefore be treated as approved on every market sharing the same pull provider.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is approved by a pull provider on market A. 2) Attacker calls `deposit` on market B, which uses the same pull provider. 3) `_tryGetCredential` calls `getCredential(attacker)` on the provider, which returns the same timestamp, and the hooks contract accepts it, marking the attacker as a known lender on market B.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-market credential reuse allows an approved lender on one market to bypass access controls on all other markets using the same pull provider, undermining per-market allowlisting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass `address(this)` and `block.chainid` to `getCredential` and require the provider to return a credential bound to those values, or maintain per-market approval state in the provider.

hypotheses.title: Withdrawal batch payment uses stale scaleFactor, overpaying early withdrawers
hypotheses.description: When a withdrawal batch is paid, `normalizedAmountPaid` is computed as `mulDiv(scaledAmountBurned, state.scaleFactor, RAY)` using the scaleFactor at the moment of payment. However, the batch's `scaledTotalAmount` was recorded at queue time, and interest continues to accrue on the unburned scaled amount until the batch is fully paid. Because `_getUpdatedState` accrues interest up to `block.timestamp` before calling `_applyWithdrawalBatchPayment`, the scaleFactor used is the current one, but the batch's `scaledTotalAmount` was fixed at queue time. This means the normalized amount paid per scaled token is higher than what the lender would have received at queue time, and the difference is effectively paid by remaining lenders (whose scaled balances are diluted). The borrower pays interest on the full scaled supply until burn, so the accounting is internally consistent, but the timing of payment (partial payments across multiple batches) lets early batches capture interest that should accrue to the whole supply.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Lender queues a large withdrawal batch. 2. Borrower partially repays over time, triggering `_applyWithdrawalBatchPayment` at each step. 3. Each partial payment uses the current (higher) scaleFactor, so the batch's `normalizedAmountPaid` grows faster than the batch's share of interest. 4. Remaining lenders' scaled balances are diluted because `scaledTotalSupply` is reduced by the burned amount but the normalized value paid out exceeds the proportional share.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair distribution of interest between withdrawing and remaining lenders; remaining lenders receive less than their fair share of accrued interest.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the scaleFactor at batch creation and use it (or a weighted average) when computing normalized payments, or accrue interest only up to the batch expiry for the batch's scaled amount.

hypotheses.title: HooksFactory.getMarketParameters is callable by anyone, leaking params
hypotheses.description: `getMarketParameters()` reads transient storage `_tmpMarketParameters` and returns the parameters for the market currently being deployed. Transient storage is only valid within the same transaction, but the function is `external view` with no access control. During a `deployMarket`/`deployMarketAndHooks` transaction, any contract called by the hooks instance (e.g. via `onCreateMarket`) can call `getMarketParameters()` and observe the parameters. More importantly, the market constructor itself calls `IHooksFactory.getMarketParameters()` via `staticcall` to `caller()` — but the factory's `getMarketParameters` is a public function that any external caller can invoke at any time. Since transient storage is cleared at end of tx, this is only exploitable within the same tx, but a malicious hooks template (deployed by an approved borrower) can read the parameters mid-deployment. The real issue is that the market constructor trusts `caller()` to be the factory and reads parameters via `staticcall` — if the factory's `getMarketParameters` returns stale/empty data (e.g. called outside a deployment), the market would be constructed with zeroed parameters. However, the market is only deployed via `create2WithStoredInitCode` inside `_deployMarket`, so `caller()` is always the factory and transient storage is set. The exposure is that `getMarketParameters()` is publicly callable and returns whatever is in transient storage, which during a deployment includes the borrower's parameters — not a direct loss but an information leak and a potential integration hazard if any external contract relies on it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious hooks template (requires being an approved borrower). 2. During `deployMarket`, the factory calls `hooksInstance.onCreateMarket(...)`. 3. The malicious hooks contract calls `IHooksFactory(factory).getMarketParameters()` and reads the transient parameters. 4. Alternatively, any contract called during the deployment tx (e.g. the asset token's `transferFrom` hook) can read the parameters.
hypotheses.impact: Information leak of market parameters during deployment; potential for a malicious hooks template to observe and manipulate deployment state. No direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `getMarketParameters()` to be callable only by the market being deployed (e.g. check `msg.sender == computeMarketAddress(salt)`), or make it internal to the factory and pass parameters via constructor args.

hypotheses.title: repayAndProcessUnpaidWithdrawalBatches is permissionless and can be used to grief
hypotheses.description: `repayAndProcessUnpaidWithdrawalBatches(uint256 repayAmount, uint256 maxBatches)` is `public` with no access control. Any caller can supply `repayAmount > 0` (pulling their own tokens) and force processing of up to `maxBatches` unpaid withdrawal batches. While processing batches is generally beneficial, an attacker can use this to force the market to process batches in a specific order/timing, potentially front-running a borrower's intended repayment or manipulating which batch gets paid first when liquidity is scarce.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a pending unpaid batch and a borrower about to repay. 2. Attacker calls `repayAndProcessUnpaidWithdrawalBatches(1, maxBatches)` with a tiny repayment, forcing the market to process unpaid batches using current liquidity before the borrower's repayment lands. 3. This can change which batch is paid and how much, potentially leaving a batch the attacker prefers unpaid.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing / ordering manipulation of withdrawal batch payments; can delay or reorder payments to specific lenders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict to borrower or a trusted keeper, or require that the caller is the borrower when `repayAmount > 0`.

hypotheses.title: collectFees is permissionless and can be front-run to deny fee recipient
hypotheses.description: `collectFees()` has no access modifier — any external actor can call it. It transfers `withdrawableFees` to `feeRecipient`. While funds go to the correct recipient, an attacker can call it at any time, including immediately before the fee recipient intends to collect, potentially causing the fee recipient's own transaction to revert with `revert_NullFeeAmount()` or `revert_InsufficientReservesForFeeWithdrawal()`. More importantly, an attacker can force fee collection at a moment when the market is about to become delinquent, reducing liquidity and potentially triggering delinquency.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker monitors the market for accrued protocol fees. 2. Attacker calls `collectFees()` right before a large borrower repayment or right before the market would otherwise become delinquent. 3. Fees are drained to `feeRecipient`, reducing `totalAssets` and potentially pushing `liquidityRequired() > totalAssets()`, marking the market delinquent and triggering penalty fees on the borrower.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: forced fee collection can trigger delinquency penalties on the borrower and cause the fee recipient's own collection tx to revert.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `collectFees` to `feeRecipient` (or borrower), or accept permissionless collection as intended and document the delinquency risk.

hypotheses.title: updateState is permissionless and can be used to force interest accrual timing
hypotheses.description: `updateState()` is `external` with no access control. Any caller can force the market to accrue interest, process expired withdrawal batches, and update delinquency status at an arbitrary time. This lets an attacker force a withdrawal batch to be processed (burning scaled tokens and reserving liquidity) at a moment of their choosing, or force delinquency status updates that trigger penalty fees on the borrower.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a pending expired withdrawal batch. 2. Attacker calls `updateState()` to force `_processExpiredWithdrawalBatch`, which burns scaled tokens and reserves liquidity for the batch. 3. This can be timed to reduce `borrowableAssets` right before the borrower intends to borrow, or to trigger delinquency penalties.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: forced batch processing and delinquency updates at attacker-chosen times; can deny borrower borrowing or trigger penalties.
hypotheses.recommendation: This is likely intended as a permissionless keeper function; if so, document it. Otherwise restrict to borrower or a keeper role.

hypotheses.title: getAvailableWithdrawalAmount rounds down per-account, allowing dust griefing of batch
hypotheses.description: The view computes `newTotalWithdrawn = batch.normalizedAmountPaid * status.scaledAmount / batch.scaledTotalAmount` with floor rounding. The comment admits dust accumulates in the batch. Because `_executeWithdrawal` uses the same formula, an account with a very small `scaledAmount` relative to `scaledTotalAmount` can have `normalizedAmountWithdrawn == 0` and revert with `revert_NullWithdrawalAmount()`, permanently locking that account's share in the batch (the batch can never be fully drained of that account's claim).
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deposits a tiny amount, queues a withdrawal in a batch alongside large withdrawals. After the batch is paid, the attacker's proportional share rounds to 0, so `executeWithdrawal` reverts. The attacker cannot recover the dust, and the batch's `normalizedAmountPaid` retains an unclaimable remainder.
hypotheses.impact: Small lenders' funds permanently locked; batch accounting shows paid but funds remain unclaimable, effectively donating to the market.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow zero-amount withdrawals to succeed (skip transfer) or accumulate dust to a claimable pool; alternatively round up the per-account share.

hypotheses.title: First depositor can inflate scaleFactor via donation to grief subsequent depositors
hypotheses.description: `_depositUpTo` mints `scaledAmount = scaleAmount(amount)` where `scaleAmount` uses `rayDiv` (round half up). If the first depositor deposits 1 wei, `scaledAmount = 1e27 / scaleFactor`. A subsequent depositor depositing a small amount may get `scaledAmount == 0` and revert with `revert_NullMintAmount()`. More importantly, the market's `totalAssets()` is `asset.balanceOf(address(this))`, so any direct donation to the market inflates `totalAssets` without changing `scaledTotalSupply`, but since `scaleFactor` is only updated via interest accrual (not via balance), donations do not directly affect `scaleFactor`. However, the first depositor can deposit 1 wei, then the borrower (or anyone) donates assets, and `borrowableAssets`/`liquidityRequired` computations use `totalAssets` — the first depositor's `balanceOf` remains 1 wei while the market holds more, and subsequent depositors' scaled amounts are computed against the same `scaleFactor`, so no direct inflation attack. The real risk is the `revert_NullMintAmount()` griefing: a first depositor with 1 wei scaled balance can be front-run by a donation that makes `scaleAmount(amount)` round to 0 for small deposits.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deposits 1 wei as first depositor. Then attacker (or anyone) donates a large amount of asset directly to the market. A victim depositing a small amount gets `scaledAmount == 0` and reverts. Victim's deposit is blocked until they deposit a larger amount.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing of small depositors; denial of service for deposits below a threshold that grows with scaleFactor.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum scaled mint (e.g., revert if `scaledAmount < MIN_SCALED`) or seed initial supply; alternatively use a virtual offset in `scaleAmount`.

hypotheses.title: applyProtocolFee uses scaledTotalSupply * scaleFactor * feeRay, overcharging on pending withdrawals
hypotheses.description: `protocolFee = scaledTotalSupply.rayMul(scaleFactor.rayMul(protocolFeeRay))` charges the protocol fee on the entire scaled supply, including tokens in pending withdrawal batches (`scaledPendingWithdrawals`). Those tokens are still accruing interest to lenders (by design), so charging protocol fee on them is consistent with interest accrual. However, `scaledTotalSupply` includes tokens that have been queued for withdrawal but not yet burned; the protocol fee is added to `accruedProtocolFees` which is subtracted from `borrowableAssets` and `withdrawableProtocolFees`. This is intended, but the rounding in `rayMul` (half-up) applied twice can over- or under-charge by up to 1 wei per accrual, and repeated accruals compound. Over many small accruals (e.g., every block), the protocol fee can drift from the true value.
hypotheses.attackPath: A borrower or fee recipient cannot directly exploit this, but a lender can call `updateState()` every block to force many small accruals, each rounding half-up in the protocol's favor, slowly draining value from lenders to the protocol beyond the intended bips.
hypotheses.impact: Lenders lose a small amount of interest to rounding; protocol gains dust. Not a direct theft but a systematic bias.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a single `mulDiv` with the combined rate, or round down protocol fees to favor lenders.

hypotheses.title: queueWithdrawal uses scaleAmount(amount) rounding up, letting users withdraw more than deposited
hypotheses.description: `scaledAmount = state.scaleAmount(amount).toUint104()` uses `rayDiv` which rounds half up. A user withdrawing `amount` gets `scaledAmount` rounded up, meaning they burn slightly more scaled tokens than the exact proportional amount. This favors the protocol (remaining lenders), not the withdrawer, so it is not exploitable for profit. However, `queueFullWithdrawal` uses `account.scaledBalance` directly, so a user can withdraw their full balance without rounding loss. The asymmetry means partial withdrawals are slightly penalized, which is acceptable but worth noting for accounting consistency.
hypotheses.attackPath: No profitable attack; the rounding favors the protocol. A user could avoid the rounding by using `queueFullWithdrawal` instead of `queueWithdrawal`, but that is intended behavior.
hypotheses.impact: Negligible dust loss to withdrawing users on partial withdrawals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document the rounding direction; consider rounding down `scaledAmount` in `queueWithdrawal` to favor users, or leave as-is since it favors the protocol.

hypotheses.title: `_getUpdatedState` uses `totalAssets()` mid-function allowing donation-based manipulation
hypotheses.description: `_getUpdatedState` reads `totalAssets()` (i.e., `asset.balanceOf(address(this))`) multiple times while computing `availableLiquidityForPendingBatch` and applying withdrawal batch payments. Because the underlying asset balance can be increased by anyone via a direct ERC20 `transfer` to the market, an attacker can donate tokens to the market right before a state-mutating call to inflate `availableLiquidity`, causing a larger portion of a pending withdrawal batch to be burned/paid than the borrower actually repaid. This shifts value from remaining lenders to the withdrawing batch.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (a lender in a pending withdrawal batch) transfers a small amount of `asset` directly to the market. 2) Attacker calls `updateState()` or any function that triggers `_getUpdatedState`. 3) `availableLiquidityForPendingBatch` sees the inflated balance and pays more of the batch, burning more scaled tokens at the current scale factor. 4) Attacker then executes their withdrawal and receives a larger share; remaining lenders' claims are diluted.
hypotheses.impact: Value transfer between lenders; remaining lenders' redeemable amounts are reduced.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track repaid/available liquidity via an internal accounting variable rather than reading `asset.balanceOf` directly, or exclude unsolicited donations from `availableLiquidityForPendingBatch`.

hypotheses.title: `_tryGetCredential` accepts future-dated credential timestamps from providers
hypotheses.description: The function reads a `credentialTimestamp` from an external role provider and only rejects it if it is zero or greater than `block.timestamp`. It then computes `provider.calculateExpiry(credentialTimestamp) >= block.timestamp`. A malicious or buggy provider that returns a timestamp equal to `block.timestamp` (or slightly in the past) with a large TTL grants effectively permanent access. More importantly, the check `credentialTimestamp > block.timestamp` allows a timestamp exactly equal to `block.timestamp`, which combined with `satAdd` to `type(uint32).max` can produce indefinite credentials. The same pattern exists in `FixedTermLoanHooks._tryGetCredential`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers as a role provider (requires borrower action, so this is only exploitable if a provider is compromised or malicious). 2) Provider returns `credentialTimestamp = block.timestamp` for any account. 3) `calculateExpiry` saturates to `type(uint32).max`, granting permanent access. 4) Attacker deposits/withdraws freely.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized access to gated markets if a provider is malicious or compromised.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `credentialTimestamp < block.timestamp` (strictly) and cap the resulting expiry to a reasonable maximum.

hypotheses.title: `onSetAnnualInterestAndReserveRatioBips` reads `intermediateState.reserveRatioBips` as original, ignoring hook-provided value
hypotheses.description: The hook ignores the `reserveRatioBips` argument passed by the borrower and always returns `intermediateState.reserveRatioBips` as the new reserve ratio (unless a temporary excess ratio is active). This means a borrower calling `setAnnualInterestAndReserveRatioBips` cannot actually change the reserve ratio when this hook is used, and the `_reserveRatioBips` parameter is silently discarded. While this is documented behavior for the constraint hook, it can surprise integrators and effectively locks the reserve ratio at its initial value, which may be undesirable if the initial value was set too low.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor; the borrower is the only caller. However, a borrower who intended to raise the reserve ratio to protect lenders cannot do so, leaving the market under-collateralized relative to intent.
hypotheses.impact: Reserve ratio cannot be increased by the borrower, potentially leaving lenders exposed to under-collateralization.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either honor the borrower-provided `reserveRatioBips` (subject to bounds) or document clearly that the parameter is ignored.

hypotheses.title: Stale view of pending withdrawal batch during hook callback
hypotheses.description: `_queueWithdrawal` calls `hooks.onQueueWithdrawal(accountAddress, expiry, scaledAmount, state, ...)` BEFORE decrementing `account.scaledBalance`, adding to `batch.scaledTotalAmount`/`state.scaledPendingWithdrawals`, and writing `_withdrawalData` and `_state`. A malicious hook template (or role provider invoked via the hook) that re-enters view functions like `getWithdrawalBatch(expiry)` or `getAvailableWithdrawalAmount` sees the pre-queue values, so the queued amount is not yet reflected. The view also runs `_calculateCurrentState`, which processes expired batches and re-reads `totalAssets`, so a hook that manipulates the underlying asset balance during the callback can further corrupt the view.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys/uses a hooks template whose `onQueueWithdrawal` calls back into an external protocol that reads `getWithdrawalBatch`/`getAvailableWithdrawalAmount`; the external protocol prices something incorrectly because the attacker's just-queued withdrawal isn't yet accounted for. If the hook can also trigger asset transfers (only if hooks template calls `asset`), it can amplify inconsistencies via `totalAssets()`.
hypotheses.impact: Dependent protocols may misprice pending withdrawals, calculate wrong available liquidity, or allow over-withdrawal against the market's stale batch values, causing fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the `hooks.onQueueWithdrawal` invocation to after all withdrawals-related state mutations and `_writeState`, or make views reentrancy-aware.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy in balanceOf/totalSupply during repay hook
hypotheses.description: `repayAndProcessUnpaidWithdrawalBatches` transfers tokens first, then calls `hooks.onRepay(...)` after computing `state = _getUpdatedState()` but BEFORE processing and writing the new `unpaidBatches`/state. During `onRepay`, a malicious hook can re-enter view functions (`balanceOf`, `totalSupply`, `getUnpaidBatchExpiries`, `getWithdrawalBatch`) and read pre-repayment, pre-batch-processing state. `_transfer` and `deposit` in other users' transactions are guarded by `nonReentrant`, but views are only blocked by `nonReentrantView` while a market state-changing call is on the stack — the hook runs within `repayAndProcess...`'s `nonReentrant`, so views DO revert here. However `totalAssets()` and any external integration calling e.g. `asset.balanceOf(market)` directly sees the updated asset balance but the stale scaled pending withdrawals. This mismatch can be exploited by a callback that reads the market's *underlying asset* balance directly.
hypotheses.attackPath: Hook re-enters an external contract that reads `IERC20(asset).balanceOf(market)` and compares it to `market.totalSupply()`. Because asset.balanceOf has already increased (repay already transferred) but market view functions revert in the same tx, an integration reading only `asset.balanceOf` will over-credit the market's recovery, allowing the attacker to manipulate a dependent liquidity/AMM position.
hypotheses.impact: External consumers of the market's underlying-asset balance see an inflated balance while market views are blocked, allowing arbitrage against integrations that rely on direct token balance queries.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform `hooks.onRepay` after all state processing and `_writeState`, so no window exists where underlying balance and market state disagree.

hypotheses.title: Hooks data suffix is not bound to the market or function selector
hypotheses.description: The hooks calldata construction copies the trailing bytes of the market call (`extraData`) verbatim into the hooks call, without including the market address, the function selector, or a nonce. The hooks contract (`AccessControlHooks`/`FixedTermLoanHooks`) then interprets those bytes as a provider address plus credential data. Because the same `extraData` suffix is valid for any market function that forwards it (deposit, transfer, queueWithdrawal), an attacker can reuse a credential payload captured from one call on a different call or market, as long as the provider accepts it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a valid `extraData` suffix (provider + signed credential) in a deposit transaction on market A. 2) Attacker replays the same suffix on a `transfer` or `queueWithdrawal` call on market B that uses the same hooks instance. 3) The hooks contract forwards the suffix to the provider, which returns the same timestamp, and the attacker is granted access.
hypotheses.impact: Credential payloads can be replayed across functions and markets, bypassing per-function access controls and allowing unauthorized transfers or withdrawals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include the market address and function selector in the data passed to the provider, and require the provider to sign over them so the credential is bound to a specific call context.

hypotheses.title: Escrow release does not verify caller or re-check sanction status atomically
hypotheses.description: `releaseEscrow` checks `canReleaseEscrow()` (which calls `sentinel.isSanctioned(borrower, account)`) and then transfers the full balance to `account`. The check is not atomic with the transfer: if the sentinel's sanction status changes between the check and the transfer (e.g., via a reentrant call or a Chainalysis update in the same block), the escrow can be released to a sanctioned account. More importantly, the function has no access control, so any external actor can call `releaseEscrow` at any time the account is not sanctioned, forcing the escrow to send funds to the account even if the borrower intended to keep them escrowed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors a sanctioned account's escrow. 2) When the account's sanction status is lifted (or overridden by the borrower), the attacker calls `releaseEscrow` before the borrower can act. 3) The escrow transfers the full balance to the account, which may be a different party than the borrower intended (e.g., if the account is a contract that has been compromised).
hypotheses.impact: Escrowed funds can be released to the account at a time not chosen by the borrower, potentially sending funds to a compromised or unintended recipient.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `releaseEscrow` to the borrower or sentinel, and re-check `canReleaseEscrow()` immediately before the transfer.

hypotheses.title: Sanction override is per-borrower and can be set by any caller
hypotheses.description: `overrideSanction` sets `sanctionOverrides[msg.sender][account] = true` for any caller, with no check that `msg.sender` is a registered borrower or that the caller has any relationship to `account`. Any external actor can therefore mark themselves as a borrower and override the sanction status of any account, causing `isSanctioned(borrower, account)` to return false for that (attacker-controlled) borrower. While this does not directly affect other borrowers' markets, it allows an attacker to create a market (if they are a registered borrower) and bypass sanctions for accounts they control.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers as a borrower (or is already registered). 2) Attacker calls `overrideSanction(victimAccount)` to set the override for their own borrower address. 3) Attacker deploys a market using their borrower address and deposits/withdraws on behalf of `victimAccount`, bypassing the Chainalysis sanction check for that account.
hypotheses.impact: Sanctioned accounts can be used to interact with markets controlled by the attacker, undermining the sanctions enforcement mechanism.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `overrideSanction` and `removeSanctionOverride` to the borrower of the relevant market, or require the caller to be a registered borrower and bind the override to a specific market.

hypotheses.title: Protocol fees accrue on scaledTotalSupply including pending withdrawals
hypotheses.description: `applyProtocolFee` computes `protocolFee = scaledTotalSupply * scaleFactor * protocolFeeRay`, i.e. protocol fees are charged on the entire scaled supply, including tokens that are pending withdrawal (`scaledPendingWithdrawals`). Lenders who have queued a withdrawal still hold scaled tokens until the batch is paid, and they continue to accrue interest — but the protocol fee is also charged on their balance. This is arguably intended (they still hold tokens), but the fee is deducted from the market's assets before the withdrawal batch is paid, reducing the liquidity available to pay the batch. Since `liquidityRequired` includes `accruedProtocolFees`, the borrower must maintain reserves for both the withdrawal and the fee, but the fee is effectively taken from the pool that would otherwise pay the withdrawal.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Lender queues a large withdrawal. 2. Time passes; protocol fees accrue on the full scaled supply including the pending withdrawal. 3. When the batch is paid, `availableLiquidityForPendingBatch` subtracts `accruedProtocolFees`, reducing the amount available to pay the batch. 4. The batch may be underpaid, and the lender receives less than expected.
hypotheses.impact: Lenders with pending withdrawals receive less than their fair share; protocol fees are effectively taken from withdrawal reserves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Exclude `scaledPendingWithdrawals` from the protocol fee base, or accrue protocol fees only on the portion of supply not pending withdrawal.

hypotheses.title: Delinquency fee accrues on full supply including pending withdrawals
hypotheses.description: The delinquency fee is applied to the entire `scaledTotalSupply` via the scaleFactor increase, including tokens in pending withdrawal batches. Lenders who have queued a withdrawal continue to accrue delinquency fees (as part of the scaleFactor) until their batch is paid. This means the borrower pays delinquency penalties on amounts that are effectively being withdrawn, and the penalty is distributed to all lenders including those who are leaving. More importantly, the delinquency fee increases the scaleFactor, which increases the normalized amount owed to pending withdrawal batches, potentially making the market more delinquent and creating a feedback loop.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Borrower becomes delinquent. 2. Lenders queue withdrawals. 3. Delinquency fees accrue on the full supply including pending withdrawals, increasing the scaleFactor. 4. The pending withdrawal batch's normalized amount owed grows, increasing `liquidityRequired` and worsening delinquency.
hypotheses.impact: Borrower pays penalties on withdrawn amounts; market can spiral into deeper delinquency; lenders who withdraw late capture penalties accrued on early withdrawers' balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Exclude `scaledPendingWithdrawals` from the delinquency fee base, or freeze the scaleFactor for pending withdrawal amounts at queue time.

hypotheses.title: closeMarket can leave unpaid batches with no mechanism to pay them
hypotheses.description: `closeMarket` processes unpaid batches using `availableLiquidity`, but if `availableLiquidity` is insufficient to pay all unpaid batches, the function reverts with `revert_CloseMarketWithUnpaidWithdrawals()` only if `state.scaledPendingWithdrawals != 0`. However, the loop over `unpaidBatches` calls `_processUnpaidWithdrawalBatch` which uses `availableLiquidity` and reduces it. If the batches are not fully paid, `scaledPendingWithdrawals` remains non-zero and the function reverts. This means the borrower cannot close the market while there are unpaid batches, which is intended. But the issue is that after closing, `annualInterestBips` is set to 0 and `reserveRatioBips` to 10000, yet unpaid batches may still exist if they were fully paid in the loop. The real flaw: if `availableLiquidity` is exactly enough to pay all batches, the market closes, but any subsequent shortfall (e.g., from rounding) leaves lenders unable to withdraw because the market is closed and no new liquidity can be added (repay reverts on closed market).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Borrower closes market with just enough liquidity to pay all batches. 2. Rounding in `_applyWithdrawalBatchPayment` leaves a tiny dust amount unpaid. 3. `scaledPendingWithdrawals` is non-zero, so `closeMarket` reverts — but if it somehow passes, lenders with dust cannot withdraw because `repay` reverts on closed markets.
hypotheses.impact: Lenders' funds frozen; market cannot be closed or lenders cannot withdraw dust amounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow repayment on closed markets to clear remaining unpaid batches, or ensure `closeMarket` handles dust by writing off or reserving it.

hypotheses.title: Sanctioned account's queued withdrawal can be executed by anyone, bypassing block
hypotheses.description: `executeWithdrawal` is public and can be called by anyone for any `accountAddress`. If the account is sanctioned, the funds are sent to an escrow contract. However, the escrow's `releaseEscrow` can only be called by anyone, and it checks `canReleaseEscrow()` which returns `!isSanctioned(borrower, account)`. The borrower can override the sanction via `overrideSanction`, which would allow the sanctioned account to receive funds. But the real issue: a sanctioned account's withdrawal can be executed by a third party, moving funds to escrow. If the sanction is later lifted (or overridden by borrower), the funds are released to the sanctioned account. This is intended. The flaw is that `executeWithdrawal` does not check if the caller is authorized, so a griefer can force execution of a sanctioned account's withdrawal, moving funds to escrow prematurely. This is not a direct loss but can disrupt the sanctioned account's ability to accrue interest (since the batch is paid and tokens burned).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Sanctioned account has a pending withdrawal batch. 2. Attacker calls `executeWithdrawal(sanctionedAccount, expiry)`. 3. Funds are moved to escrow, tokens burned, interest stops accruing for the sanctioned account.
hypotheses.impact: Sanctioned account loses future interest; funds moved to escrow without consent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `executeWithdrawal` for sanctioned accounts to the borrower or a trusted party, or allow the sanctioned account to opt out.
